answer: DefaultJSONProvider in src/flask/json/provider.py has an ensure_ascii attribute that defaults to True. Its dumps() passes that value through to json.dumps, so by default every non-ASCII character in serialized output is escaped as a \uXXXX sequence and the output is pure ASCII. Setting app.json.ensure_ascii to False keeps Unicode characters literal in the output string, which is more compact and readable but changes the bytes sent over the wire. The response helper app.json.response() and jsonify() go through the same provider, so the setting applies to all JSON responses produced by the app. Tagged session serialization in json/tag.py is a separate path that does not read this flag.

The flag is Blueprint._got_registered_once, set to True inside Blueprint.register() in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py. Every setup method (route, add_url_rule, before_request, errorhandler and similar) is wrapped with the setupmethod decorator, which calls self._check_setup_finished(f_name). That check raises an AssertionError when the flag is set, with a message naming the method and the blueprint, so a blueprint cannot gain new routes or hooks after it has been attached to an app. The point is that deferred setup functions are replayed once per register() call, so late additions would silently never run for apps that registered earlier. Calling the same blueprint on a second app is still allowed, because the check is on the blueprint's own state.

Static serving is implemented in both the app and the blueprint, in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py. Scaffold.__init__ sets static_folder and static_url_path, and when a static folder is configured it registers a route whose view is send_static_file. For the app, the endpoint is named static; for a blueprint the endpoint is the blueprint name plus .static and the rule is prefixed with the blueprint url_prefix. Both call flask.helpers.send_from_directory, which calls get_send_file_max_age() and reads the SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT config key. In Flask 2.0 and later the default is None, which means no fixed max-age, so responses carry validators (ETag and Last-Modified) and clients revalidate conditionally. Because both components share that one helper and config key, caching behaves identically for app static files and blueprint static files.

The class is flask.debughelpers.UnexpectedUnicodeError, defined in src/flask/debughelpers.py. It subclasses both AssertionError and UnicodeError. Flask raises it in debug-oriented code when form or file data is accessed with an enctype that does not match the request body, and the bytes cannot be decoded or are binary rather than text. The UnicodeError base reflects the actual failure, which is a decoding problem. The AssertionError base marks it as a developer-facing programming or validation mistake rather than a client input problem, so it is treated as a bug signal during development. Inheriting from both lets code that catches encoding errors and code that catches assertion failures both handle it, which keeps the encoding layer and the validation layer distinct while still letting one exception type describe the problem.

The test is test_subdomain_basic_support in tests/test_basic.py. Its dependency chain runs in three stages. First it sets app.config['SERVER_NAME'] to a host such as localhost, which the app reads when building its URL map and when computing the subdomain prefix. Second it registers routes with a subdomain argument on app.route or add_url_rule, and those rules are stored in app.url_map, a werkzeug Map that compares each rule's subdomain against the request host. Third it calls app.test_request_context() with a base_url or subdomain, which builds a WSGI environ carrying HTTP_HOST and creates a RequestContext. That context creates a MapAdapter via url_map.bind_to_environ, and the adapter matches the request path and subdomain against the rules to choose the endpoint. The test asserts both the matched rule and the generated URL.

Blueprint template processors are recorded as deferred setup functions. Blueprint.context_processor(f) in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py calls record_once or record to append a closure that does app.template_context_processors.setdefault(self.name, []).append(f) when the blueprint is registered. App-wide processors are stored under the key None. At render time, render_template calls app.update_template_context(context), which in src/flask/sansio/app.py builds the list of names from request.blueprints (the active blueprint chain) plus None, and runs every processor found under those keys, merging their results into the context. Those processors are shared across all templates rendered by app.jinja_env, the one shared Jinja environment. So a processor registered on a blueprint only applies while a request is routed to that blueprint, and it does so through the shared environment without any per-blueprint environment.

The test helper is a small class in the test suite that implements __fspath__, which is the os.PathLike protocol. When the standard library calls os.fspath(), pathlib conversion, or open() on such an object, Python calls __fspath__ and uses its return value as the path. The method returns the path string the helper was built with, usually a plain str, and Python requires that the result be a str or bytes. Because this is the protocol hook, the test verifies that Flask accepts any PathLike object wherever it accepts a path, for example in config loading such as from_file or from_pyfile. The exact class name is in the test module; the answer is that __fspath__ returns the stored path string.

The test is in tests/test_cli.py and is parametrized over import_name and app_name values that should not resolve to an app. It calls flask.cli.locate_app(import_name, app_name, raise_if_not_found=True). That function imports the module with prepare_import and then looks for an app by name, first checking a variable with the given name and then, when no name is given, the names app and application, and finally any single Flask instance. When nothing matches, it raises NoAppException with a message that tells the user what to set. The parametrization makes every bad combination of module and name fail through the same exception path, so the CLI reports one consistent error and exits instead of producing a traceback. The test asserts that exception type across all cases.

FlaskCliRunner in src/flask/testing.py subclasses click.testing.CliRunner. Its invoke() method builds a ScriptInfo whose create_app callable returns the test's Flask instance, and passes it as the obj argument, so the click context carries the app. When a command needs the app, it calls ScriptInfo.load_app(), which uses the create_app callable instead of importing an app path, and then reads app.cli. The base CliRunner.invoke runs the command in isolation by swapping stdin and stdout and catching SystemExit, so the result object exposes exit code and output without touching the real process. The chain is therefore: the test app instance goes into FlaskCliRunner, into ScriptInfo.create_app, into ScriptInfo.load_app, and finally into the Click command invocation provided by CliRunner.

The recursion runs through TaggedJSONSerializer in src/flask/json/tag.py. The TagTuple class's to_json method maps each element through self.serializer.tag(item). TaggedJSONSerializer.tag() loops over its registered tag objects in order, calls each tag's check(value), and when one matches it calls that tag's to_json, which calls tag() again on the children. So tag() and to_json() recurse through the structure. A tuple can only contain a cycle through a mutable object such as a list or dict nested inside it, because tuples are immutable. Nothing in the module tracks visited objects, so a circular reference causes unbounded recursion and eventually a RecursionError. The serializer does not detect cycles, so the caller must avoid circular structures in the session or JSON data.

I could not verify the exact test class from the README, which only covers the project overview. Based on what I know of Flask's tests, the streaming tests in tests/test_basic.py and related context tests in tests/test_reqctx.py use a class-based pattern that sets up an app and a test client, then exercises flask.stream_with_context around a generator that reads request data. The architectural idea is that the request context is pushed and popped by the test harness as a separate lifecycle, while the generator's execution happens after the view function has returned. The tests isolate the two so that a streamed body can still access request and session data even though the view's own frame has finished. Treat this as a best guess about the class and its exact structure.

The coupling is between the decorator's registration state and the request context's response lifecycle. After-request callbacks registered by after_this_request() in src/flask/helpers.py are appended to the current request context's _after_request_functions list, and they run later from Flask.process_response() in src/flask/app.py, not at the moment of decoration. The decorator therefore depends on being called while a request context is active, and it writes to state owned by a different object. If a decorator is applied conditionally or nested, the callback may be registered for the wrong request, run more than once, or run in a context that has already been popped. Likewise, app-level hooks added through the setupmethod decorator must be registered before the first request, so state set at decoration time and state read at response time are tied together in ways that break with late or conditional registration.

The wrapper is _lazy_sha1 in src/flask/sessions.py. It returns hashlib.sha1 applied to its arguments only when called, instead of binding hashlib.sha1 at import time. The session serializer uses it as the digest method for itsdangerous signing. On systems that run FIPS mode or otherwise restrict SHA-1, merely referencing hashlib.sha1 during import can fail or be blocked, which would stop the whole application from importing. By deferring the lookup to call time, the module imports cleanly, and the failure, if any, happens only when a signed session is actually created or verified. This moves a restricted-environment error from import time to runtime, where it is easier to handle and where only apps that use sessions are affected.

The decorator is flask.stream_with_context in src/flask/helpers.py. It takes the active request context from the context variable _cv_request, and wraps the generator so that it runs inside a with block on that context. Entering the context pushes it again for the duration of the generator's execution, so request data and the session stay available to code that runs while the response is being streamed, after the view function has returned and its own context would normally be gone. Because the context is re-pushed rather than copied, the session and request objects are the same ones that the view used, which keeps session data consistent across the execution boundary. The contextvars design means that each concurrent request or greenlet sees its own context, so streaming from one request cannot leak another request's data into the generator.

The conversion is in the CertParamType class in src/flask/cli.py, which is the click ParamType behind the --cert option of flask run. Its convert method implements a fallback chain. If the value is None, it returns None. If the value is the string adhoc, it keeps it as the marker for a generated self-signed certificate. If the value is an existing file path, it is passed through as a path for the server to load. If it is neither of those, it tries to import it as a dotted object path with werkzeug's import_string, and the resulting object is expected to be an ssl.SSLContext, which is returned as is. If all of those fail, it raises a click BadParameter error describing the accepted forms. The order matters because adhoc and file paths are cheap to check, while import is the last and most expensive resort.

Template filters registered through Blueprint.add_app_template_filter in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py are deferred. The method calls self.record_once with a closure that sets app.jinja_env.filters[name] = f. record_once runs the closure only once per app, when the blueprint is registered, and it does not depend on the blueprint's url_prefix. Because the filter goes into the app's shared Jinja environment, every template rendered by the app can use it, whether or not the blueprint's routes are active or the blueprint is mounted under a prefix. The url_prefix only affects the URL rules that the blueprint's other deferred functions add. So the mechanism is: store the filter as a deferred function, replay it on registration, and write it into the one shared environment.

TagBytes in src/flask/json/tag.py converts bytes to and from JSON. Its to_json method calls base64.b64encode on the bytes and decodes the result to ASCII text, so the JSON carries a plain string. Its to_python method reverses this with base64.b64decode, giving back the identical byte sequence. The serializer identifies the value by a tag key, a single space followed by b, which the check method looks for when untagging. Base64 is a bijection between byte sequences and its ASCII alphabet, so the round trip is lossless for any bytes, including those that are not valid UTF-8. The tag key is what makes it reversible, because without it the decoder could not distinguish a base64 string from ordinary text.

The method is Flask.handle_exception in src/flask/app.py. It is called for unhandled exceptions that escape the view and the error handler lookup. It first logs the exception through log_exception. Then it checks the propagate_exceptions property, which is True when the PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS config value is set, or when TESTING or DEBUG is enabled and it is not set explicitly. If propagate_exceptions is true, it re-raises the original exception so the debugger or test client sees the traceback. Otherwise it wraps the error in an InternalServerError, looks up its handler with _find_error_handler, and returns that response, so the client receives an HTTP 500 response. The decision therefore depends only on configuration state.

Blueprint.add_url_rule in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py does not register the rule itself. It defines a closure of the form lambda s: s.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, view_func, **options) and hands it to self.record(), which appends it to self.deferred_functions. The closure is not called at this point because the blueprint has no app yet. When the blueprint is later registered on an app, Blueprint.register() creates a BlueprintSetupState and runs each deferred function with it, and the state's add_url_rule prefixes the rule with the blueprint's url_prefix, sets the endpoint to include the blueprint name, and calls the app's add_url_rule. This lets one blueprint be mounted on several apps or with different prefixes, because the rule is replayed each time.

SecureCookieSession in src/flask/sessions.py inherits from werkzeug's CallbackDict. Its constructor passes an on_update callback that sets self.modified to True whenever a key is set or deleted. Reads set self.accessed, which tells the framework that the session was used so a Vary: Cookie header can be added. At the end of the request, SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session in the same module checks modified, and writes a new signed cookie only when the session changed, or when permanent sessions are refreshed each request. Because the cookie is the only storage, each request loads its own copy from the signed payload and no server-side lock exists. Concurrent requests therefore both start from the same cookie and the last response to set it wins, so the callback keeps memory state and the outgoing cookie in step within one request but cannot coordinate across requests.

The namespace is _AppCtxGlobals, exposed as flask.g and defined in src/flask/ctx.py. Each AppContext creates its own instance in its constructor, and the active app context is stored in the context variable _cv_app. Because contextvars are isolated per thread and per asyncio task, code running in one thread or task sees only the g object of its own app context. The object itself is a plain attribute store with no locking, so it is not safe to share one g across threads that have each pushed a separate context, but this is not needed because each request gets its own context. Concurrent requests therefore cannot see each other's values. The g object lives only as long as the app context, so data placed there is discarded when the context is popped.

The behavior is in _AppCtxGlobals in src/flask/ctx.py. Attribute reads through __getattr__ raise AttributeError for a missing name, which matches normal Python semantics and lets hasattr work. Attribute deletion through __delattr__ and the explicit remove path also raise AttributeError when the name is absent. The get method returns a default of None or a supplied value for missing keys without raising. The pop method takes a default argument, and when that default is not supplied it uses a sentinel object, so pop still raises KeyError or AttributeError for missing names unless the caller provides a default. In practice the strict methods catch typos and misuse, while get, pop with a default and setdefault give callers a safe way to read optional values.

The type is defined in src/flask/typing.py. The main alias is ResponseReturnValue, a union that lets a view return a Response, a string, bytes, a dict, a list, a generator, or a tuple of body, status and headers. Dictionaries are typed as dict[str, Any] and are converted by make_response through the app's JSON provider, which serializes them with app.json.response. The HTTP status is not part of the dictionary. It is supplied as a separate tuple element, typed through the StatusCode alias, and headers are typed as HeadersValue. So the JSON body and the status code are separate parts of the return value, and the type system checks each one on its own. Tests in tests/type_check check that route functions returning dict or list of dict type-check correctly.

View.__init_subclass__ in src/flask/views.py handles the methods attribute. The methods list tells Flask which HTTP verbs a view class handles. The hook runs when a subclass is created. If the subclass does not define methods in its own __dict__, it collects the methods sets from all direct base classes, then adds the upper-cased name of each HTTP method the class defines as a function, such as get or post. The result is assigned to cls.methods when it is non-empty. This means that a child inherits and extends the parents' verbs instead of losing them, and an explicit methods attribute on the child is left alone. The merge is a union across bases, so when several parents declare methods the child gets all of them.

TagUUID in src/flask/json/tag.py converts uuid.UUID values to and from JSON. Its to_json method returns value.hex, a 32-character string with no hyphens. Its to_python method builds a new uuid.UUID from that string. The tagged serializer is used for session data, and JSON on its own has no UUID type, so without the tag a UUID stored in the session would come back as a plain string. Making the conversion bidirectional means that a value written to the session is read back as the same UUID type, and the tag key, a space followed by u, tells the decoder to rebuild it. The hex form is chosen because it is compact and canonical, and it round trips exactly.

The async class is flask.views.MethodView subclasses that define async handlers, and the reason it reuses the synchronous dispatch base is that the dispatch logic is the same. Method lookup by HTTP verb, the methods attribute, and the metaclass that collects handlers are all unchanged. The only difference is whether the handler returns a coroutine. Flask already handles that difference in the app: View.dispatch_request returns whatever the handler returns, and Flask.ensure_sync in src/flask/app.py wraps coroutine functions with asgiref's async_to_sync when they are called from the sync WSGI path. Duplicating dispatch in an independent async class would copy the verb routing and the methods handling, which would then have to be kept in step with the sync version. Inheriting keeps one implementation and lets the async behavior come from ensure_sync.

ScriptInfo in src/flask/cli.py accepts create_app and app_import_path as alternative ways to produce the app. The app_import_path form is what the command line uses. The --app option supplies a string such as module:name, and ScriptInfo imports it lazily when a command needs the app. The create_app callable form is for programmatic use, where a test or an embedding program already has a factory function and wants the CLI to call it without going through an import string. Both feed the same load_app method, which checks create_app first and falls back to the import path. Giving both options lets the same CLI group serve command-line users, tests through FlaskCliRunner, and code that embeds the CLI, without each caller reimplementing app discovery.

Scaffold.open_resource in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py resolves a resource name against the object's root path, using get_root_path, and then opens it with the built-in open. It restricts the mode argument to read modes, rb, r and rt, and raises ValueError for any other mode. The reason is that resources belong to the installed package or application directory, which is often read-only or shared, and the method's purpose is to read bundled data such as templates, configuration or static files. Permitting write modes would let a caller modify package files from application code, which is unsafe and surprising. Restricting to reads keeps the method's contract narrow and makes its behavior predictable across installs. The method returns the file object for the caller to read and close.

ScriptInfo in src/flask/cli.py stores the imported application in a private attribute, _loaded_app, and load_app creates the app only the first time it is called. This is lazy loading. The reason is ordering. When flask runs, the command group is constructed before its options are parsed, and the --app value, the environment, and the debug setting are not available at construction time. Importing the app during __init__ would run the user's module before those values are known, and it would also run module-level side effects when a user only asks for --help. Deferring the import to load_app, which is called from the command callback after parsing, lets the cache hold one app per invocation while keeping construction cheap and side-effect free.

SecureCookieSession in src/flask/sessions.py overrides __getitem__ and related read methods to set self.accessed to True on every read. The attribute is a plain Python assignment, so its own cost is small, but the flag has consequences for every response. Once accessed is set, the response gets a Vary: Cookie header, and the session interface does extra work to decide how to handle the cookie. Setting it unconditionally in a hot read path means that code which only reads a value still pays for the flag assignment and changes the response headers, even though nothing was written. In a loop over many reads, the repeated assignment and the cache-sensitive header logic add up. The cost is modest per read, but it is paid on every access, which is why the performance concern shows up under frequent reads.

Blueprint-level template filter registration in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py uses add_app_template_filter, which records a deferred function with record_once. Each call appends a closure to the blueprint's deferred list, and when the blueprint is registered each closure writes an entry into the app's shared jinja_env.filters dictionary. If the same filter registration is repeated across many distinct blueprint objects, the cost grows linearly with the number of blueprints, because each blueprint has its own deferred list and its own replay during register. Each replay is a dictionary write, so the cost is small, but at startup with many blueprints and many repeated filters it adds up, and the same filter name is written again and again. The sensible fix is to register a shared filter once on the app rather than repeating it per blueprint.

The test is in tests/test_blueprints.py and checks that a Blueprint name containing a dot is rejected. The check is in the sansio Scaffold or Blueprint constructor in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py. It tests whether the name contains a '.' character and raises ValueError with the message that names may not contain a dot. The reason is that Flask builds endpoint names as blueprint_name.view_name, and the dot is the separator between the blueprint part and the view part. A dot inside the blueprint name would make endpoint names ambiguous, so url_for and the error handler lookups could not tell where the blueprint name ends. Rejecting the dot at construction time turns that silent routing ambiguity into an immediate, clear error.

SecureCookieSessionInterface.get_signing_serializer in src/flask/sessions.py builds a new itsdangerous URLSafeTimedSerializer on each call, with the app's SECRET_KEY and the salt and digest method. Creating that serializer derives a signing key from the secret through a key derivation step that runs HMAC over the salt, which is a comparatively expensive operation. Because the method is called for every request on both the open and save paths, each request repeats the derivation even though the inputs never change for a given app. Under high concurrency, that repeated CPU work per request is multiplied across all workers and becomes a bottleneck. Caching the serializer, or building it once per app, would remove the repeated derivation without changing the cookie format.

PassDict in src/flask/json/tag.py is the tag class for plain dictionaries that do not need a special tag. Its to_json method returns a new dict in which each value is passed through self.serializer.tag, while the keys are copied unchanged. The reason keys are not tagged is that JSON object keys must be strings, and the serializer never needs to attach type information to them. The only data that needs a tag is the value, which might be a tuple, bytes or UUID. Tagging a key would also be unnecessary and would break the format, because untagging looks for a single-key dict with a tag name as its key. Dictionaries whose only key happens to start with the tag marker are wrapped in a separate TagDict escape so that user data is not mistaken for a tag.

The test is in tests/test_logging.py. It sets up a stream handler on the root logger and then checks how Flask's logger behaves. The app logger created by create_logger does not get its own default handler when a handler is already reachable from the root logger, because the helper has_level_handler walks up the logger hierarchy and finds the root's StreamHandler. The test asserts that app.logger.handlers is empty. That shows Flask avoids adding a duplicate handler, which would cause each message to print twice, and relies on propagation to the root handler instead. The empty list is the expected result, not a missing value. The behavior means that applications which configure logging at the root level get their output once, through the existing handler.

The root path is changed in make_config, a method of the App class in src/flask/sansio/app.py that Flask.__init__ calls. When instance_relative_config is true, make_config uses the instance path in place of the root path before it creates the configuration object. Concretely, it sets root_path to self.instance_path, and then constructs the Config with that value. The Config object stores that path and uses it to resolve relative files such as from_pyfile and from_file. So the instance path substitution happens inside make_config, before the value reaches the Config storage object. The flag itself is set by the constructor argument, and the change applies only to configuration file loading, not to the rest of the app's root path use.

The control flow is in FlaskGroup.get_command in src/flask/cli.py. It first calls the superclass get_command, which returns a command registered directly on the group with the decorator or add_command. If that returns nothing, it falls back to the commands loaded from the flask.commands entry point group. Those plugin commands are gathered by _load_plugin_commands, which runs once when the group is set up. If there is still no match, it loads the application through ScriptInfo.load_app and asks the app's own cli group, app.cli, for the command. The order is directly registered commands, then entry point commands, then application CLI commands. The first match wins, so a command registered on the group shadows the same name from a plugin or from the app.

The serializer class is TagMarkup in src/flask/json/tag.py. Its to_json method calls the object's __html__ method, which Markup provides, and converts the result to str. Its to_python method returns a markupsafe.Markup object built from the stored string. The helper functions that do the work are markupsafe's Markup and its __html__ protocol. Markup is a str subclass that marks text as already escaped, so the tag must keep it as Markup rather than plain str to avoid double escaping in templates. The tag check is isinstance against the Markup type, and since Markup is a subclass of str, the check order in the serializer matters so the Markup tag runs before the generic string handling.

TagList in src/flask/json/tag.py handles list values. Its to_json method returns a new list in which each item is passed to self.serializer.tag(item). That call is the place where the item conversion meets the serializer's type dispatcher. The serializer's tag method walks its ordered list of tag objects, checks each one's check method against the item, and uses the first one that matches, which can be a dict, tuple, bytes, datetime, UUID, Markup or another tag. Because each item is dispatched again, nested lists and mixed structures are processed recursively, with each level choosing its own tag. The untagging side mirrors this through the object_hook, so lists of mixed types round trip through the same ordered dispatch.

The routing control flow is split between src/flask/sansio/app.py and the request dispatch in src/flask/app.py. When add_url_rule registers a view, it checks the view function's provide_automatic_options attribute. If that attribute is missing, and OPTIONS is not already among the methods, the rule gets provide_automatic_options set to True and OPTIONS is added to the required methods. Werkzeug then routes OPTIONS requests to that rule. At dispatch time, Flask.dispatch_request checks whether the request method is OPTIONS and the matched rule has provide_automatic_options set, and if so it calls make_default_options_response instead of the view. The flag can be overridden per view by setting the attribute on the function, and the app-level configuration sets the default behavior.

The lookup is in _find_error_handler in src/flask/sansio/app.py. It takes the exception and the list of active blueprint names. It computes the exception's HTTP code, if it has one, and then walks a fixed sequence. For each scope in the blueprint names, innermost blueprint first, then None for the app-wide scope, it checks the handlers registered for the specific status code, then the handlers registered for the generic None code. Within each of those, it walks the exception class's method resolution order, so a handler for a base exception class matches a subclass. The first handler found is returned. So the order is blueprint scope, then status code, then exception class MRO inside each code, and the app-wide handlers come after the blueprint ones.

I could not confirm the exact file and class from the README, which covers only the project overview. Based on my knowledge of Flask's test layout, URL building tests with anchors, schemes and HTTP methods are in tests/test_basic.py, in a class around url_for and in the url building tests that use _external and the scheme and anchor keyword arguments. Treat the exact class name as a best guess. The tests exercise Flask.url_for in src/flask/app.py and the werkzeug MapAdapter.build behind it, checking that anchor fragments, the _scheme argument and method-specific rules produce the expected URL. Please verify the class name in the repository before relying on it.

I could not verify this from the README. Based on what I know of Flask 3.1, the resource opening method is Scaffold.open_resource in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py. It builds the full path by joining the resource name to the object's root path, obtained from get_root_path, and then calls the built-in open with the requested mode. The test that passes an encoding would call the method with that argument only if the method accepts it, and in Flask 3.1 the documented signature is open_resource(resource, mode='rb'), so text decoding is normally done by the caller or by opening in text mode. Treat the detailed flow of an encoding parameter as uncertain and check the test source before relying on it.

Base64 decoding for bytes tags is done by TagBytes.to_python in src/flask/json/tag.py, which calls base64.b64decode. It is invoked during untagging. TaggedJSONSerializer.loads calls json.loads with object_hook set to the serializer's untag method. After the JSON parser builds each object, the hook is called with the decoded dictionary. untag checks the dictionary for a single key that matches a registered tag, and if it finds one it calls that tag's to_python. For a bytes value the key is the tag for bytes, and that routes the value into TagBytes.to_python, which decodes the base64 string back to bytes. So the decoding happens inside the JSON object hook, while parsing, not in a separate pass afterwards.

The inheritance relationship is handled by Config.from_object in src/flask/config.py. The method accepts a class or module object and iterates over dir(obj), which includes attributes inherited from base classes, so a child configuration class sees the parent's uppercase settings. For each name that is all uppercase, it reads the value with getattr, which applies normal Python attribute resolution, so a child that overrides a value supplies its own, and a child that does not override it gets the parent's value. Only uppercase names are copied into the config, so lowercase helpers are skipped. The result is that a config class hierarchy resolves to the most derived value for each key, and the loaded config contains the merged view.

The orchestration sits in Flask.wsgi_app in src/flask/app.py. It creates a RequestContext, and calls ctx.push(), and push in src/flask/ctx.py calls the session interface's open_session, which loads the signed cookie into a SecureCookieSession. The view runs, and then Flask.full_dispatch_request and finalize_request call process_response, which calls save_session on the session interface to write a new cookie if the session was modified. Concurrency is handled by the design, not by locks. Each request works on its own session object loaded from the cookie that the browser sent, and no server-side store is shared. Two concurrent requests can both read the same cookie and each write a new one, and the last response to arrive wins, so the framework does not protect against lost updates between simultaneous requests.

The route handler is in the type check test files under tests/type_check, for example typing_route.py, where a function decorated with @app.route returns a list of dictionaries. The route decorator is App.route in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py, which is typed with overloads and the ResponseReturnValue alias from src/flask/typing.py. The static type checker, mypy or pyright, is configured through the project's configuration file, which sets the strictness and test paths, and the test files are checked as part of the type check suite rather than run at runtime. The check confirms that the decorator accepts a view returning list[dict[str, ...]] as a valid ResponseReturnValue, so a regression that narrows the return type would fail the type check. This is a best answer based on the layout of the type check directory, and the exact file names should be confirmed in the repository.

The linear walk is in _find_error_handler in src/flask/sansio/app.py. For each lookup it iterates the exception's __mro__, and for every class it performs a dictionary lookup in the error handler spec for each blueprint scope and for the app-wide scope, and for both the status code and the None code. So the number of dictionary lookups is roughly the MRO length times the number of scopes times two. Python computes the MRO once per class, so the traversal is just a sequence of hash lookups, which is cheap. The overhead matters only for very deep hierarchies combined with many blueprints and many registered handlers, and it happens only on the error path, not on normal requests. In typical applications the cost is negligible, and the cost could be reduced by caching the resolved handler per exception class.
